subject: dwarfBlacksmith
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: dwarf blacksmith at an anvil.
Style: Blizzard/Warcraft.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a full module, aiming for something substantial since I can't test it interactively, so I need to be careful with the SDK API usage. The subject is a Warcraft-style dwarf blacksmith at an anvil—chunky exaggerated proportions, huge pauldrons, braided beard, hammer, apron, and a glowing hot sword blade on the anvil.

I'm now designing the humanoid rig, roughly 1.4m tall with oversized hands and broad shoulders, positioning the anvil in front of the dwarf at the origin, facing forward with arms raised toward the anvil in a working pose. I'm building the spine chain with hip, chest, and spine joints using a catmull curve, naming each segment appropriately.

For the torso, I'm deciding to use lofted geometry with sweeps along the bone chains rather than individual joints, connecting the hip and spine bones to form the body shape.

Now I'm roughing out the dwarf's proportions in meters: overall height around 1.45-1.5m with helmet, hips at y=0.5, and short thighs/shins plus boots to keep the stature compact.

For the legs, I'm computing hip-to-foot IK distances to figure out knee bend—using leg segment lengths around 0.24 each gives a slight forward knee bend rather than a straight leg, which looks more natural. I'm setting up each leg as a three-point chain (hip, knee, ankle) that I'll sweep for the mesh geometry.

I'm sorting out the side convention—deciding to use world coordinates consistently so that positive X maps clearly to "left" and naming joints with L/R suffixes accordingly, avoiding confusion between local and world space when mirroring the two legs.

Now I'm sketching the proportions for the dwarf's head and torso: a short neck with a big head centered around y≈1.13, broad shoulders at ±0.27 width, and estimating overall height with a chunky helmet bringing the total to roughly 1.3+ meters, consistent with a stocky Warcraft-style dwarf build.

I'm working out how to build the skull shape and face features, using a scaled sphere for the head and planning to use decals for the eyes positioned along the front surface of the skull rather than separate geometric parts.

For the dwarf's eyes specifically, I want small, deep-set almond shapes with bright blue irises placed slightly off-center and low on the face to suggest a heavy brow. Now I'm thinking through the nose and brow ridge as additional sculpted sphere/box parts.

For the beard, I'm planning a classic Warcraft dwarf style with braided sections ending in metal rings — building this with swept geometry along curved paths, stacked ellipsoid plaits for the braid segments, and a tapering main beard mass hanging from the jaw down over the chest, rigged to the head bone despite its length.

I'm working out joint attachment logic: keeping mustache and main beard mass on the head bone for simplicity, with a smaller chin goatee piece attached to the jaw so it moves naturally when the mouth opens. Now I'm setting up the neck-to-head joint chain using a catmull spline with named joints spanning from neck to head.

Defining more joints...

Setting up the spine chain...

Still shaping torso profile and sizing shoulders with pauldrons, then settling on an Ironforge dwarf color scheme: dark blue tunic, brown leather apron, steel pauldrons trimmed in gold.

Now I'm designing shading helpers for skin and cloth, writing a lighting function that mixes warm and cool tones based on surface normal direction to give the forge-lit dwarf a believable glow.

Then I'm scoping out the overall part count, aiming for around 200 pieces, including textures for eyes, hair strands, beard fur cards, anvil/hammer runes, and an apron emblem with a hammer-and-anvil crest.

Now I'm working out the key body proportions: head center and radii, neck and chin positions, torso span from hips to chest, and shoulder width, so the dwarf's overall height and silhouette stay consistent as I lay out the components.

Shoulder joints branch from the chest, and I'm chaining arm segments from shoulder to elbow to wrist to hand. Rather than a strict symmetric rest pose, I'm positioning the right arm raised holding a hammer and the left arm extended forward gripping tongs, placing the anvil just in front of the dwarf to anchor the scene.

The anvil sits on a short stump, with the anvil body rising from about waist to belly height, oriented with its horn pointing sideways along the X axis so the working face is accessible from where the dwarf stands.

I'm working out arm reach: with shoulder-to-hand segments around 0.22 each, the hand positions land close to target distances, so I'll set the right hand (holding the hammer) near [-0.30, 0.86, 0.40] and the left hand (holding tongs) near [0.26, 0.80, 0.42], placing the workpiece on the anvil's top surface right at the near edge where the dwarf can strike it.

Now I'm positioning the tongs' bar from the left hand toward the anvil surface, and figuring out the hammer's orientation so the head rests cocked above the workpiece rather than pointing somewhere awkward -- picking a haft direction from the grip so the head lands roughly above the strike point for a natural swing pose.

I'm working out that the hammer head's axis should sit perpendicular to the haft within the swing plane, so in the cocked position the striking face angles back and up rather than straight down.

Now I'm figuring out how to attach the hammer rigidly to the hand bone, then build out the arm joint chain for the rig.

Simplifying to just a fingers joint and thumb joint per hand, each tagged as digit roles. For the look, I'm leaning into a dwarf blacksmith aesthetic: sleeveless bare arms with leather bracers and steel vambraces, gloves in brown leather, with the upper arm thicker than the forearm tapering toward the wrist.

Adding bracer bands as a separate sweep...

Now thinking about shoulder pauldrons — layered armor plates like big Warcraft-style shoulders, built from a hemisphere scaled with a gold trim torus ring and a spike cone, positioned to follow the shoulder joint as the arm moves.

Adding a gold rim torus and rivets to the pauldron, then moving to torso clothing: a deep blue tunic with a leather apron draped from chest to knees. I'm working out how to wrap the apron around the rounded belly, considering a loft-based sweep with front stations along the spine instead of a flat extrude that would clip through the body.

This flat loft approach won't hug the body well, so I'm reconsidering: maybe build the apron from membrane surfaces between loop edges sliced to the front arc, stitching consecutive torso loops together directly instead of a separate flat cross-section.

Rather than fitting loops through the pelvis sphere, I'll simplify by treating the lower apron as hanging cloth: an upper apron built from the membrane over torso loops lifted slightly, and a separate flat extruded skirt piece hanging freely from the belt down toward the knee, since cloth naturally drapes that way regardless of underlying geometry.

I'm weighing whether to use the membrane-loop approach for the torso, checking that slicing planes at various y-values avoid cutting through arm meshes since they're separate sweeps, and figuring out how to close the loop path with a world-up direction for the apron contour.

Now I'm setting rows at different heights with varying half-width fractions to shape the bib narrower at the chest and wider at the belly, keeping the membrane thin for a subtle contour.

I'll chain four membranes between consecutive row pairs, using leather-paint coloring and letting bone weights inherit from the path's default surface skinning. For the sliced sections, I need to confirm that slicing a closed path yields open sub-paths that concatenate properly, with slice bounds running from (1-width) to 1.

Then I'm adding a belt as a swept loop lifted slightly above the belly, dark leather colored, with a gold buckle plate at the front—something like an anvil-emblem centerpiece with studs running along the strap for detail.

I'm setting the hit region on the belt to sit at front-center on the torso surface, then moving on to the lower skirt flap and the bib straps draped from the chest over the shoulders to the back, letting the drape function pull them naturally onto the torso surface. I'll make sure the heavy beard covers the upper chest area, hiding where the straps attach at the top, and I'm adding a shoulder yoke detail to the tunic before moving to the legs—dark trousers with thick leather boots and a chain-skinned sweep for the leg tubes.

Now I'm figuring out the chunky Warcraft-style boot geometry: a shaft piece rising from the ankle joint, and a horizontal frustum box for the foot running from heel to toe, sized so the sole just touches the floor without sinking too far in. I'm working out the exact center height and thickness so the boot bottom lands right at y=0, and considering which axis the frustum box's width should run along for a boot shape oriented horizontally.

Then I'm layering in details: a steel toe cap as a slightly enlarged front box in a contrasting color, a thin dark sole, and a leather or fur cuff ring around the top of the boot using a rotated torus oriented horizontally. For the legs, I'm planning a radius-varying sweep along the hip-knee-ankle chain to form trousers that taper where the boots begin, plus knee pad caps attached at the nearest point on the leg sweep surface in front of the knee joint.

For the pelvis I'm using a scaled sphere at the hip bone colored to match the trousers, with legs starting from the hip joints. For the head, I'm leaning toward a dwarf blacksmith aesthetic: a steel/bronze half-sphere skullcap with a gold band, small curved tusk-like side horns, a red mohawk crest on top, and brass goggle lenses pushed up on a forehead strap — keeping it simple rather than overloaded.

Now I'm working out the facial features: a reddish-orange beard and mustache, ears poking out beside the head with earrings, a bulbous ruddy nose with tiny dark nostril spheres, thick bushy brow ridges made from angled capsules or cone-shaped bristles, cheek spheres, eye decals, and a hidden mouth under a big curling handlebar mustache with a lower jaw box for structure.

The beard itself needs texture, so I'm planning hair strand cards with tapered gradient shapes (dark root to bright tip) scattered across the beard surface for fluffiness, layered over a solid sweep-based mass that paths down from the chin toward the chest, since dwarf beards traditionally run long toward the belly.

I'm positioning the beard mass so it sits in front of the torso without clipping into it, calculating the sweep radius and path points so it tapers from chin to a point above the belt, then adding two braided side-strands hanging alongside the main beard.

Actually, I'm reconsidering the shape to avoid the braids clashing with the main beard mass — narrowing the central beard with mutton-chop sides and starting the two braids lower down, each ending with a gold ring, built as ellipsoid segments following a curved path aligned to the tangent direction.

Simplifying to a zig-zag chain of small spheres offset left/right along local axes to fake a three-strand braid, rather than true helix sweeps.

I'll attach the beard to the head explicitly since it should move with head rotation, and I'll always pass an explicit bone rather than relying on nearest-joint detection for safety. Now working out the braid link geometry...

For the braid I'm using a scaled, slightly asymmetric ellipsoid with alternating orientation to fake a twisted look, since true roll isn't available. I'll finish the braid with a torus and cuff cylinder in gold plus a tuft cone at the end, and sweep the mustache with a catmull curve.

Now I'm working out precise head coordinates: center at (0, 1.2, 0.06) with radii roughly 0.155/0.145/0.15, placing the nose near (0, 1.17, 0.225), eyes at y=1.225 offset ±0.058 in x, and mouth around y=1.12. I'm tracing the mustache path outward and slightly upward from under the nose, curling the ends near (±0.17, 1.12, 0.12) with a tapering radius from 0.032 down to 0.016.

I'm defining a symmetric sideburn-and-jaw path that sweeps from near the ears down through the cheeks to the chin, using a thick radius around 0.05, then checking whether points along that path actually fall inside the head ellipsoid by plugging coordinates into the ellipsoid equation to see if the sum of squared ratios exceeds 1.

The beard tube needs to cup the jawline, but the jaw itself has to remain a separate skin-colored piece hidden mostly by beard, with a small goatee tuft and a dark mouth slot box placed near the lower lip to suggest the hidden mouth beneath the mustache.

Computing where eye decals should sit on the skull sphere's surface—roughly 10° elevation and 20° azimuth from head center gives placements near the right x and y offsets for symmetric eyes.

I'm sketching the eye texture itself: a small almond shape with pale blue iris, dark pupil, highlight dot, a thick brow-shadow line, and under-eye bagging to match the gruff dwarf look, mirroring left/right while keeping brow slant for an angry expression. Now I'm working out where to place the brow ridge rod relative to the eye socket.

Still shaping the eyebrows...

For the head, I'm layering the skull sphere with added cheekbone spheres and a forehead shape, then extruding pointed ear forms positioned on either side with thickness built into the cross-section.

Still placing ear geometry... now adding a gold torus earring and starting the helmet with a dome cap scaled and positioned over the forehead.

Checking the cap's bottom edge geometry against the eyebrow position reveals a collision at the front, so I'm adjusting by tilting the cap backward with a rotation around the x-axis to clear the brows.

Still sketching the horn and crest geometry...

Overall head height lands around 1.48-1.5m, fitting a stocky Warcraft-style dwarf proportions. I'm thinking about adding goggles to the cap front -- brass lens cylinders tilted upward with a subtle blue glow.

Now I'm figuring out the strap and brim placement using loop geometry around the cap, picking a y-coordinate near the cap's lower edge since it's tilted, and deciding whether to use a torus for the brim band instead.

I decide to settle on a uniform torus radius with a slightly thicker tube to hide the mismatch, then shift focus to planning efficient helper functions — mirroring parts across axes, caching sphere geometries, and a generic ball-part builder with flat shading and color constants — so I can scale up to 200+ parts without excessive repetition.

Now I'm defining the paint palette: a mottled, countershaded skin tone for warmth and belly shading, a shaded blue mottle for cloth, and a grainy countershaded leather texture, all built as layered paint wrappers to keep variety without blowing past color limits.

I'm bringing in the metal helper from the clockwork kit along with a glow helper, then assigning gilt, brass, steel, iron, and blued finishes to the various metal parts like trim, hammer head, and armor pieces. For hair I'm using a directional grain paint in warm orange tones with darker countershading beneath, and a similar grain approach for wood textures, while planning the anvil as dark iron with high contrast highlights.

Now I'm sketching out the anvil's construction from box segments and tapered forms: a base foot, a waist frustum, a top plate forming the face, a horn cone, and a tail step, all centered around a defined anvil point. I'm also planning a wooden stump base with bark texture and ring detailing on top, plus an iron band wrapped around it near the base.

Adjusting the horn's spike dimensions so its base radius and center align properly with the face top at 0.8, keeping it thin and proportioned.

Now I'm placing the tail/heel section as a horizontal frustum on the opposite side, adding the hardy and pritchel holes, and setting up materials — a polished steel top face and dark iron body — plus a gold Dwarven rune mark on the anvil's side.

I'm positioning a glowing rune plaque on the anvil's front face (the side toward the dwarf) with warm orange glowing text, then setting up a glowing metal workpiece — likely a sword blade being forged — lying across the anvil between the dwarf's tongs and the hammer's strike point.

I'm positioning the bar extending along −X with its glowing tip over the anvil center, and working out the hammer's cocked-up position in the raised hand relative to the hand coordinates.

Calculating the head axis direction, I find it points back-up-outward, with the strike face roughly aligned toward the anvil center, which checks out geometrically. Now I'm sketching the hammer head geometry itself, using a short cylindrical shape with octagonal cross-section for the main body.

Still writing hammer geometry...

I'm also sketching the tongs for the left hand -- two crossed rod arms pivoting near the bar, with handles extending back past the hand and jaws meeting at the grip point.

The glowing blade blank itself I'm positioning lying flat on the anvil face, tang held by the tongs around x=0.1, stretching out toward a tapered tip, while the hammer stays positioned above near the strike point.

Since paint materials can't glow uniformly across a gradient, I'm splitting the blade into three separate extruded segments by x-range — a hot yellow-orange tip, a cooler red-orange midsection, and a dark non-glowing steel base — each needing its own outline polygon generated by a helper function.

Defining tip geometry...

For extra effect, I'll add small glowing spark particles flying around the hit point, maybe a dozen tiny glowing cubes plus embers. I'll skip adding a forge or ground since the brief only mentions an anvil.

For the character, I'll skip props not explicitly named, keeping just a hammer and tongs. I'll add belt pouches and a hammer-loop to the leather apron, plus a small gold hammer-and-anvil emblem decal on the apron bib using a decal applied to the apron's surface.

Since beard coverage reaches down to about 0.78 on the chest, the emblem placement needs to move lower, onto the skirt flap of the apron instead of the chest center, and I'll be careful with typing to avoid unused variable errors given the apparent strict typecheck.

Shortening the main beard to end around y=0.8 opens space for the emblem around y=0.68, tucked between the side braids at ±0.1, with the apron decal spanning roughly 0.56 to 0.98 — though I'll need to shift the belt position slightly to avoid overlap.

I'm skipping extra surface details like chest hair or scars, keeping the design simple with a torus collar ring at the neck base and sleeveless arms covered by leather bracers and pauldrons. For rigging, I'm laying out the full joint hierarchy — hips, spine segments, chest, neck, head, jaw, shoulders down through fingers, and legs to the toes — while deciding which joints actually need dedicated roles.

Now I'm working through chain parenting, like attaching the arm chains to the chest joint and positioning the shoulders symmetrically, then figuring out how the limb-building helper returns joint points that feed directly into the chain function as a polyline.

I'm now reasoning through elbow and knee bend directions—setting hints so elbows angle outward and back, knees bend forward—and double-checking the limb lengths and target distances for both legs and arms to make sure the resulting joint angles look natural.

Checking the left hand's reach, I find the target is too far from the shoulder for the given arm length, so I pull it in closer to a reachable position, while also considering the shoulder joint's placement relative to the torso width and adding a deltoid muscle ball to cover the socket. I'm also setting up the hand geometry, with the left hand gripping tongs via a palm box and finger shapes.

Designing fist shapes and grip poses...

Simplifying the fist grip idea: wrap a flat-sided cylinder around the haft as the fist shape, then add a few bump-like finger ridges on the front side rather than a full ring of sphere knuckles.

Generalizing a gripFist helper for the tongs, computing the handle direction from hand to the bar point and splaying the two rods with a perpendicular offset so they converge near a pivot point before reaching the jaws.

Still working out scissor geometry...

Working out the geometry for the handle and jaw rods meeting at the pivot, with a rivet sphere at the joint and thicker grip cylinders wrapped around the handle ends near the hand position.

Checking clearances: anvil width against blade and hand positions looks fine, torso-to-anvil distance clears the knees, and the stance width works for the standing legs. I want to make sure feet and stump bottoms sit flush with the floor, then I'll add some finishing details like a gold belt buckle, pouches, and a hammer loop before nailing down the exact torso dimensions.

I'm sweeping the torso profile along the spine curve with varying rx/ry radii to shape the belly and shoulders, but I'm realizing the rounded end cap at the top would use the shoulder radius and stick up too high above the neck — I need to shrink the cap radius there to avoid an oversized dome.

Switching to a flat top cap solves the shoulder issue since neck and pauldrons will cover that area, but the round start cap at the bottom extends further than the pelvis sphere and could poke out visibly between the legs. I'm leaning toward making both caps flat and letting the pelvis mesh handle the coverage instead.

Now I'm adding deltoid lumps and a collar sphere near the top of the chest to round out the shoulder transition, plus a neck rod connecting the chest to the head base.

For the tunic, I'm going with ironforge blue, sleeveless so the arms show bare. For the beard, I'm designing a hair tuft texture card tapering from dark orange base to lighter tip with streak details, then scattering dozens of these cards along the beard's downward flow direction.

Now I'm working out the beard's main sweep geometry, defining a catmull-rom path of points descending from the chin with varying radii to taper the shape toward the tip.

I want low-poly facets for the hair, using fewer sides and flat shading instead of smooth. I'm also planning a forked beard tip, with the main beard splitting into two lobes that sweep outward and taper to points, plus separate hanging braids from the sides.

Checking the braid coordinates against the beard mass dimensions, I realize the braids float too far from the belly surface since the z-depth doesn't match the belly's front curve—I need to pull the braid z-values inward to follow the belly contour instead of the wider beard depth.

I'm also adding hair details for the back of the head: a hidden sphere beneath the cap for visible nape hair, plus a thick hanging braid down the back for a nice silhouette from behind.

Now I'm sketching the armor pieces: a beard surface built from a sweep path, pauldron plates with spiky clusters as the Warcraft-style hallmark, and steel vambraces with gold banding at the forearms. I'm skipping a bandolier to keep things simpler, and noting that all paints operate in a shared model-space so texel density stays consistent across parts.

Writing geometry helpers...

I'll settle on a color type alias for flexibility, and decide bone weighting should be mostly rigid with smooth chains for the torso. Now I'm starting to write out the actual implementation code.

Importing the builder utilities and kit modules...

Still defining material palettes...

Now I'm planning the remaining texture assets: eye, hair tuft, an emblem of hammer and anvil on a shield for the apron, a glowing rune plaque for the anvil, stump growth rings, a subtle glow texture for the hammer head, and simpler flat-color or glow treatments for goggles lenses, sparks, and the belt buckle (reusing the emblem texture).

Writing SVG code...

Adding iris highlights and lid shadow...

Now I'm checking stroke widths relative to icon size, then sketching a separate tuft/hair piece with a gradient fill transitioning from dark auburn to bright orange.

Moving on, I'm designing a shield-shaped emblem with a dark blue field, gold border, and an anvil-and-hammer glyph inside.

Still writing SVG code...

Next I'm sketching a transparent rune plaque with dark backing and glowing orange glyph strokes, keeping the background cutaway dark while the glyphs themselves glow.

I'm reconsidering the hammer rune placement—adding a small glowing orange glyph texture on the sunken plate of the hammer head's side face, figuring out which local axis points toward the haft attachment direction to orient it correctly.

Now moving to the rigging setup: I'll define the joints first before building the body parts, starting with a hips joint as the root/first spine joint, then building out the spine chain as a polyline of joint positions upward from the hips.

Continuing the joint chain upward from the chest into the neck, head, and jaw, each positioned and aimed to connect naturally with the parent joint below it.

Now I'm setting up the arm loop for left and right sides, defining shoulder positions and per-side hand targets, then building the limb through intermediate bend points for the forearm shape.

I'm chaining shoulder, elbow, and hand into a named arm bone group with proper parenting, then defining a sweep function to taper the arm thickness along its length.

Still defining joint helpers...

Still working out the normal vector math...

Positioning the thumb capsule using a perpendicular offset vector, then deciding on bare skin-toned fists with big ruddy dwarf knuckles and leather wrist cuffs rather than full gloves.

Now I'm working through the leg rig: computing hip-to-ankle joint chains with tapered thigh/calf sweep radii, trouser coloring, and figuring out where the boot shaft should start relative to the knee height.

Rigging the boot on the ankle bone with a frustum foot box from heel to toe, a steel toe cap with a rounded sphere tip, a thin sole, a fur-lined cuff torus at the top, and a small gold buckle detail.

Now I'm adding a toe joint under the ankle for digit articulation, placing a ball-shaped pelvis part at the hips, and designing steel knee pad plates positioned forward of the knee joint with a flattened sphere shape oriented along the leg's normal direction, plus a gold trim ring.

For the torso I'm planning leather harness straps that cross from shoulders down to the back with a buckle detail, and considering whether to add a back-hung tool or hammer for extra character detail.

I decide on a bedroll instead: a horizontal cloth cylinder strapped to the upper back, tan-colored, keeping it simple with just the roll and straps. Now I'm starting to write the actual build function...

Writing build function...

Still working out the sweep and surface setup for the torso, then building apron membrane geometry from loop points along the surface...

Now I'm building the apron membranes between arcs with consistent winding direction, then adding stitched seam trims as thin dark-brown sweeps along the boundary arcs for a leatherwork detail.

Next I'm sculpting the belt as a closed hexagonal sweep around the torso loop at the waist, with a thinner secondary strand layered on top, then placing a stick-mounted buckle box oriented along the surface normal to sit flush against the belt.

Embedding onto the moved frame at 0.2. For the buckle emblem, I realize stick/part accept a texture parameter mapped to the geometry's UVs, so a box can show the emblem art directly on its face—using a small plate box with the EMBLEM texture, backed by a slightly larger gold ring box for framing.

Now I'm positioning an apron emblem decal around y=0.68, checking it clears the belt top at 0.60 and sits above the beard tip at 0.76, with the braids at x±.11 not overlapping its half-width of .065. I'm setting up the decal call targeting the apron front surface near z=0.25, and flattening the apron parts into an array to pass as the decal's target meshes.

Next I'm sketching shoulder strap paths using a draped Catmull-Rom sweep from the front bib over the shoulder to the back, checking the sample points land near the torso's surface including the flat shoulder cap, and considering a box-shaped cross-section for the strap sweep radius.

Now I'm defining the strap dimensions and adding shoulder anatomy: cloth yoke spheres covering the chest/shoulder region, deltoid balls attached at the shoulder joint, and a pauldron function that places a flattened dome-shaped steel plate at an angle on the shoulder, using a hemisphere geometry open on one side.

Working out the layering for the pauldron plates...

Adding spike and stud details...

Working out the ring-frame helper for positioning rivets, then checking that the dome pauldron's width properly covers the shoulder joint beyond the chest and arm radius. I'm also planning the forearm bracer as a steel sweep segment with flat caps and a gold accent, roughly spanning from mid-arm to just past the elbow.

Now I'm sketching thin gold bands at the bracer edges and confirming the sweep function can crop its source range and vary radius along the arm's parametric position, then moving to define the skull geometry using a soft low-poly sphere scaled to head proportions.

For the eyes, I'm computing hit points on the skull surface at symmetric angles and deciding how to orient the decal direction—considering whether to use the surface normal or force a straighter forward-facing tilt for better symmetry.

Setting roll to s*8 so ccw rotation raises the outer corner on each side for an angry look. I'm considering adding eye bags but deciding to skip them since the heavy brow already conveys enough depth, then moving on to shaping the nose with a skin-colored ball and nostril details.

Adding nostril balls, a bridging rod sweeping from brow to tip, and a ruddy mottled countershaded skin tone for the nose. Then shaping the cheeks and jaw with additional skin-colored wedges, leaving the eyebrow hair detail for later.

Now I'm placing a dark mouth slot hidden under the mustache, adding two tiny cream tusk cones poking up from the jaw for a cute effect, and a thick reddish lower lip ball to finish the mouth area.

Shaping the mustache with a curved catmull path that tapers from thick near the nose to thin curling tips, sweeping over the mouth and curling upward at the ends—then moving on to sketch out the beard sections next.

Working through the sideburn sweep tapering from narrow at top to wide mid-cheek then thin again, and deciding whether the main beard should attach to the jaw bone so it rides naturally when the mouth opens, with sideburns staying fixed to the head bone instead.

Writing beard scatter and card generation code...

Still placing the gold rings...

Now I'm sketching a braid helper that walks along a catmull spline and places alternating beads offset sideways in the local frame to create a woven look, attaching small spheres as hair parts along the bone.

For spacing I estimate link count from path length versus bead width so the beads overlap slightly for a continuous braid feel. Then I'm capping the braid end with a gold cuff cylinder and finishing it off with a small conical tuft spike positioned at the tangent of the path's endpoint.

Now I'm adding a gold bead at the start of this braid piece, then moving on to the back-head braid using similar catmull spline logic with a thicker bone-anchored strand. For the cap, I need to work out the tilt rotation so the torus orientation vector matches the intended upward-and-back angle of about 14 degrees.

I'm defining the cap geometry as a scaled partial sphere, then choosing a steel material with a panelled rivet texture for the cap, pauldrons, and bracers to give an armored look. For the goggles, I'm setting up a surface-sampling helper on the cap to position them at specific azimuth and elevation offsets relative to the cap's center.

Now I'm working out the lens assembly: brass cylindrical housings embedded into the cap surface, topped with blue-tinted glass lenses that have a subtle glow, plus a leather strap rod bridging the two lenses through the dome's interior so it stays hidden.

I'm skipping the sweep-based strap band for simplicity, then moving to pointy Warcraft-style ears extruded from the head bone, gold hoop earrings at the lobes, and now placing a belt pouch on the hip using an azimuth offset around the belt loop.

Skipping the dangling key ring and tail flap details, I'm moving to the front apron flap, defining its extrude outline with a flaring zigzag hem shape.

Now I'm positioning that skirt piece against the torso and pelvis geometry, placing it at the right depth near the belly and pelvis radius, and tilting the extrusion outward at the bottom so it angles away from the body rather than hanging straight down.

I'm checking the skirt against leg placement, making sure the width and bottom edge at knee height don't collide with where the knee and its pad sit.

I'll shorten the skirt hem slightly, dropping the outline a bit so it clears the legs, and I'll skip adding extra trim or texture details on it to keep things simple. For the hammer-blade impact, I'm planning a cluster of small glowing yellow spark boxes scattered randomly within a radius around the contact point.

For rigging, I'm reconsidering the anvil's bone attachment — since it's a static prop rather than part of the skeleton, parenting it directly to the hips would make it move unintentionally with character animation. Since only one parentless root joint is allowed, I'll restructure so a top-level `root` joint sits at the origin, with `hips` as its child for character motion, and the anvil parts attached to `root` instead so they stay fixed.

Now I'm writing the anvil geometry itself, starting with a tapered stump cylinder positioned at the base, then adding a ring of small sphere bumps around it to suggest root flares at the bottom.

Rings stay visible at the edges where the foot doesn't cover them. For the iron bands, I'm adding two tori sized to match the cylinder's tapering radius at their respective heights, placing one near the base and one higher up.

Now I'm working out the anvil shape itself: a frustum box for the foot tapering from wider at the base to narrower, then another frustum for the waist section, adjusting the dimensions so the transitions between sections feel proportional rather than abrupt.

Still placing horn and tail geometry...

Still placing holes and details...

Now sketching the blade geometry: positioning it just above the anvil's top plate, defining its glowing segments and tapering width from tip to shoulder to tang, where it'll be gripped by tongs.

Continuing the segments: 0.1-0.22 dark iron for the tang with no glow, skipping the fuller detail and glow bloom cards for simplicity. Now moving on to computing the hammer's position vectors, starting with the handle and head center coordinates.
